videos.title: Enthalpy, Entropy and Non-Equilibrium Reactions | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Explain why burning glucose and photosynthesis stay away from equilibrium, using the signs of the enthalpy change and the entropy change. Read the sign of the Gibbs free energy change (delta G) to decide whether a reaction is favoured, and keep that separate from how fast it runs. Work through the glucose example one step at a time, then compare the reverse process, photosynthesis.

0:00 The puzzle
1:05 Heat and entropy
2:28 Burning glucose
4:38 Photosynthesis in reverse
6:17 Practice question
7:18 Working through the answer
9:02 Key notes

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports analysing non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"analyse examples of non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy, for example:
- combustion reactions
- photosynthesis"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, exothermic and endothermic reactions, entropy as the spread of particles and energy, and the link between enthalpy, entropy and delta G. Next: What a flask already at equilibrium does when it is disturbed by a change in concentration or temperature.

#Year12Chemistry #Entropy #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
analyse examples of non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy, for example:
- combustion reactions
- photosynthesis

videos.description:
Squeeze a gas mixture that is sitting at equilibrium and predict which way it shifts by counting only the gas particles. Explain the shift as the side with fewer gas particles becoming favoured when every gas is more crowded. Handle equal gas counts and solids, and tell a squeeze apart from adding an inert gas at fixed volume.

videos.description:

videos.title: Calculating K: the Three Question Types and ICE Tables | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Equilibrium calculation questions come in three types. Do the first two here: substitute settled concentrations straight into K, then use an ICE table (I for initial, C for change, E for equilibrium) when you are given a start and one measured equilibrium value. Put the measured value in the equilibrium row first, work out its change as equilibrium minus initial, then use the coefficients for the other changes. Also see how K flips when the equation is written backwards.

videos.title: Temperature and the Equilibrium Constant: How Does Heat Change K? | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Adding a chemical, squeezing the container or adding a catalyst never changes K. Changing the temperature does. See why with a sealed tube of brown nitrogen dioxide: heating speeds up both reactions, but the one that takes in heat speeds up more, so the mixture settles somewhere new and K changes. Learn the rule for endothermic and exothermic reactions, and how to read it backwards from a table of K values.

videos.title: Finding Equilibrium Concentrations from K (No Quadratic Needed) | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
The third type of equilibrium calculation: you are given K and the starting amounts, and you need the equilibrium concentrations. Set up the ICE table with an unknown x, then use one of two shortcuts. If the equation is a perfect square, take the square root. If K is tiny and the start is not, drop the x from the bottom, solve by multiplying both sides by the bottom and dividing, then check that x is under about 5 per cent of the start.
